summary.text: An ideal of a ring is a special subset of its elements, generalizing subsets of the integers such as the even numbers or the multiples of 3.
Adding or subtracting even numbers keeps you among the evens, and multiplying an even number by any integer gives an even number; these closure and absorption properties define an ideal.
An ideal can be used to build a quotient ring, much as a normal subgroup is used to build a quotient group in group theory.

facts.label: Ideals of the integers
facts.value: Each is the multiples of one non-negative number

facts.label: Ideal numbers
facts.value: Ernst Kummer invented them as the missing factors where unique factorization fails

facts.label: Dedekind in 1876
facts.value: He replaced Kummer's undefined idea with concrete sets of numbers

facts.label: Kernels
facts.value: Two-sided ideals are exactly the kernels of ring homomorphisms

facts.label: Multiples of n
facts.value: All integers divisible by a fixed integer n form the ideal nℤ

items.prompt: You take any even number and multiply it by 7, or by 10, or by any other integer. Which property of the evens does this show?

options.label: Multiplying a member by any ring element keeps the result inside
Multiplying two members together always gives back a member
Multiplying a member by any ring element lands outside the set
Multiplying a member by an outside element needs an inverse

items.explain: Multiplying an even number by any integer, even or odd, gives an even number. This absorption, with closure under adding and subtracting, defines an ideal.

items.prompt: In group theory a normal subgroup is used to build a quotient group. What plays the matching role when building a quotient ring?

options.label: A field
An ideal
A rng
A polynomial

items.explain: An ideal can be used to construct a quotient ring in a way similar to how a normal subgroup constructs a quotient group.

items.prompt: You want to list every ideal of the integers. What labels them one-for-one?

options.label: The prime numbers
The even numbers
Pairs of integers
The non-negative integers

items.explain: Among the integers, ideals correspond one-for-one with the non-negative integers, each being the multiples of a single non-negative number.

items.prompt: You send a ring through a ring homomorphism and collect everything that lands on zero. What kind of subset is that collection?

options.label: A two-sided ideal
A single element only
A field
A left ideal and nothing more

items.explain: The kernel of a ring homomorphism is a two-sided ideal, and every two-sided ideal arises as such a kernel.

items.prompt: A ring has commutative multiplication. What happens to the difference between left, right and two-sided ideals?

options.label: Only two-sided ideals survive
Right ideals become the only kind
The three kinds become the same thing
Left ideals split into two new kinds

items.explain: If the ring is commutative, the definitions of left, right and two-sided ideal coincide, so one speaks simply of an ideal.

items.prompt: In some number rings, numbers do not break into factors in only one way. What was Kummer's invention meant to do about that?

options.label: Delete the numbers that factor badly
Supply imagined numbers acting as the missing factors
Replace every ring with the integers
Prove that factoring never needs extra factors

items.explain: Kummer invented ideal numbers to serve as the missing factors in rings where unique factorization fails; Dedekind later replaced them with concrete sets.
